items.title: Deadly Crash in Zimbabwe Leaves Nearly 30 Christians Dead
items.author: Tré Goins-Phillips
items.summary: Pray.
items.content:
📖 News | Faithwire

At least 27 people died and seven others were injured after a minibus taxi carrying members of a Christian congregation crashed into a haulage truck in Zimbabwe.

According to Paul Nyathi, a spokesperson with the Zimbabwe Republic Police, the truck driver was trying to pass another vehicle when he or she fatally struck the minibus taxi on Friday, about 87 miles south of Harare, the country’s capital city.

Video footage of the incident showed the taxi mangled and completely charred by flames, DW reported.

The truck in question carried foreign registration plates, which means it was not registered in Zimbabwe. The haulage vehicle was reportedly carrying mining equipment from South Africa.

As for the minibus taxi, its passengers were reportedly from the indigenous denomination the African Apostolic Church, also known as the Mwazha church. The travelers — purportedly around 34 of them — were on their way from Dema to Ndarikure in Mvuma for a faith-based conference, according to the Arabian Post.

The provincial government minister put the death toll at 23, while the remainder died at the hospital.

President Emmerson Mnangagwa declared a State of Disaster in response to the crash, invoking Section 27(1) of Zimbabwe’s Civil Protection Act. By invoking the act, the country’s government is able to invest in resources and assistance for survivors and families mourning losses.

The money can be used, too, to cover medical fees and burial costs.

Please keep the families of those who have lost loved ones in this accident in prayer.

items.title: Why Christians Must Prepare For ‘Information Warfare’
items.author: Billy Hallowell
items.summary: Important.
items.content:
📖 News | Faithwire

A communications expert who specializes in Generation Z and Christian communications is warning there’s an informational battle unfolding that believers must pay attention to — and that fears of new technologies must be tempered.

Listen to the latest episode of “Quick Start”

“New media is something we shouldn’t be afraid of,” Bethany Miller, communications director for National Religious Broadcasters, told CBN News, explaining that people both young and old are relying on social media for information and news gathering. “We need to stay ahead of the curve and realize new media is the way. Social media is how we get our headlines.”

Miller knows the pitfalls that can come from getting news from Reels and short videos, discussing how younger people are even more tuned in to social media for these purposes.

“Today’s Gen Z’s … and … teenagers … are growing up without any form of separation between the digital and the physical,” she said. “And so information is being consumed … and then the tricky part is now we’re having the question of: ‘What is real and what is not real?'”

This complicates how people process information around war and major news events, and with artificial intelligence emerging it only adds to the chaos and confusion. As a result, there’s an “information warfare” of sorts taking form.

“We’re having a type of access that’s misinformation and we’re getting headlines that are not accurate,” she said. “We’re getting everyone’s opinion and … we don’t need everyone’s opinion because now we’re having both truth and untruth and now Gen Z has a barrage — the American public as a whole has a barrage — of headlines.”

Miller continued, “And now you have to do the discernment of what is true, what is not true, and my concern is that Gen Z has not grown up with that distance between what is reality and what is not reality.”

The assumption that random videos and AI-generated content are true is creating a plethora of confusion, she said.

“Gen Z doesn’t have that type of discernment that they need to realize whether or not something is true, whether something is biblical, whether something is true, good and beautiful,” Miller said.

Despite this dynamic, she described being encouraged by how Christians are stepping into social media, film, TV, and other forms of entertainment, offering quality content. For a long time, Christian entertainment was criticized for a lack of excellence, but Miller believes those tides are changing.

“Christian media is paving the way, but we still have quite a lot more work to do,” she said, noting it’s important for Christians to get a better grip on the audience. “I think we’re starting to see that, but we still have a long way to go. We need to make sure that we know our audience. We know that 30 seconds is what performs well on Instagram. We need to know that we need to format.”

Miller added, “We know that Christian media has the answer, we have truth, we are the only ones that are providing the way to eternity.”

Part of engaging, she said, is understanding that we’re in a spiritual war that requires engagement. She cited examples of persecution in Nigeria not getting much coverage — and of Israel being maligned after Hamas’ deadly October 7 terror attacks.

“The mission field is different today,” Miller said. “When we talk about the Great Commission, that doesn’t just mean going over across seas to Africa; it also means getting online because the mission field is also media. It is also digital.”

And that digital world, much like the physical, demands that Christians take action.

“The digital world is a spiritual world as well and Christians need to be there combating, and we need to be there leading the front lines, and we need to be there getting the truth,” she said.

items.title: Skilla Baby’s Prayer Alarm Went Off on ‘The Breakfast Club,’ So the Whole Studio Stopped and Prayed With Him
items.author: RELEVANT Staff
items.summary: Skilla Baby was in the middle of an interview on “The Breakfast Club” Tuesday morning when his phone went off. It wasn’t a call. “It’s time for the prayer, too,” he said. “My prayer time.” Charlamagne tha God offered to stop. “You want to stop an
items.content:
📖 Culture | Relevant Magazine

Skilla Baby was in the middle of an interview on “The Breakfast Club” Tuesday morning when his phone went off. It wasn’t a call.

“It’s time for the prayer, too,” he said. “My prayer time.”

Charlamagne tha God offered to stop.

“You want to stop and pray? We can.”

“Yeah, come on. You’re gonna do it. Let’s do it. You’re gonna pray, or you want us to pray?”

“I want y’all to do it,” Skilla Baby said.

So the show stopped. The hosts got out of their chairs, gathered in a circle in the middle of the studio and held hands, and co-host Loren LoRosa prayed out loud.

“Dear Lord, Heavenly Father, thank you for bringing us together today. I thank you for Skilla Baby and his journey and his voice. I pray that you cover him. You continue to lead him down a path of leadership, but also down a path of vulnerability as he places his life story out for other people to see, to know, to understand, but also to follow in the right way.”

“I also pray that you comfort him in moments where we don’t even understand what comfort is, where he may not understand what comfort is, but that you sit right there next to him. You speak to him. You hold him in the ways that he is needed.”

“I pray no spirit of confusion, no spirit of fear, and I just pray that you continue to show favor in his life. I know that he is here for a reason. I know that he is still here with us for a reason.”

In May of last year, Skilla Baby’s SUV was hit with more than 25 rounds in a drive-by in Redford Township, just outside Detroit. He was struck three times and needed multiple surgeries.

He has said since that the shooting was not the hard part. Getting shot was “easy,” he told Complex, compared to the mental health battles he has had most of his life. Gospel singer Erica Campbell and her church, he has said, walked him through a dark stretch afterward.

The album he came on the show to promote is called The Price of Fame.

“Beautiful prayer, Loren,” Charlamagne said when it was over. “Skilla Baby, keep growing, my brother.”

items.title: Unsettled by Wendell Berry
items.author: Andrew Tolkmith
items.summary:
Andrew Tolkmith

Much of his life was dedicated to recovering a robust sense of what human beings are made for and striving against the most destructive impulses of the human spirit.
items.content:
📖 Catholic Teaching | Word on Fire

Andrew Tolkmith

As many as possible should share in the ownership of the land and thus be bound to it by economic interest, by the investment of love and work, by family loyalty, by memory and tradition.

—Wendell Berry, The Unsettling of America

In the coming days, weeks, and months, scores of elegies will pour into the discourse grieving the loss and celebrating the life of Wendell Berry. I am not well versed in his work; I’ve only read a tiny fraction of his mammoth output as a poet, novelist, and essayist. But I know for certain that he changed my life, and because so much of his life was dedicated to recovering a robust sense of what human beings are made for and to striving against the most destructive impulses of the human spirit, it would be discourteous not to concentrate instead on the effect his project has had on me, in this case a few rambling thoughts extended from my modest reading of him. 

Berry wanted to inspire real human change; he was a prophet who chronicled the end of a certain age in the history of mankind and saw the beginning of a new one. So it seems that rather than just reflecting on his legacy, my energies would best be put toward picking up the story he told tirelessly, toward reflecting on how the new wineskin of our age might be filled with new wine made from the fruit of his prophecy.

* * *

A driven Christian, Berry often drew attention to the parables of Christ, who frames most of them in the context of agrarian life: the barns, the wheat and the chaff, the workers in the field, the sower, the grain that cannot bear fruit unless it falls to the ground and dies. It’s reasonable to suppose that since Jesus lived in an agrarian society, he simply chose images and concepts that were close at hand, and that if he lived in another kind of society, he would have chosen other images and concepts. It’s reasonable, but I think it’s wrong. Human identity is inextricable from the land. We need to eat in order to live, and we do not eat if we do not grow food, and we do not grow food if conditions don’t support growth. No matter how advanced humanity gets, we will not survive if we do not integrate with creation.

* * *

Extend this all the way to the heart of Catholicism: the Eucharist, the source and summit of the Christian life, which Christ himself said is his flesh for the life of the world (John 6:51), cannot be confected unless wheat and grapes—the fruits of the earth—are grown, harvested, and processed into a very specific type of bread and wine suitable for the sacrifice. Let’s face it: The Church cannot be the Church unless people can ensure that the land can yield wheat and grapes and craft them into food. In a real sense, the health of our souls—the source of our union in Christ—is in the soil. How’s that for identity?

* * *

When Mary Magdalene first saw Jesus after he rose from the dead, she mistook him for a gardener. God forbid we mistake this as a mere accident or happenstance. Adam and Eve were created in a garden, they lived in a garden, they sinned in a garden, and they were damned in a garden. Could we do otherwise but discover our redemption in a garden?

* * *

We don’t have enough gardens. Practically speaking, humans are made to grow their own food. “I have given you every plant yielding seed that is upon the face of all the earth, and every tree with seed in its fruit; you shall have them for food” (Gen 1:29). Obviously we’re not all supposed to leave the city and start homesteads. Obviously we can’t deconstruct modern life and resurrect agrarian life tomorrow. But more of us could use our property to grow vegetables, and for those of us who can’t or don’t own property, why can’t we buy some pots, fill them with soil, learn how certain vegetable plants grow and how much sunlight and water they need, and grow them? Why can’t we swear off the vegetables in the grocery store and choose to depend on what we can produce on our porch? Why can’t we live by the seasons, sticking to broccoli in the spring and tomatoes in the summer? When was the last time we bought meat from a local cattle farmer? Limitations on our existence make us more human. “We have tried to escape the sweat and sorrow promised in Genesis—only to find that, in order to do so, we must forswear love and excellence, health and joy.”

* * *

Catholicism integrates every aspect of life into a harmonious whole. Wendell Berry was not Catholic, but through his account of the inner mechanisms of industrial, consumerist society, I began to grasp just how disintegrated my own life was. How especially impoverished I am because of my manicured independence from my local community! I have no meaningful relationship to the land that I live on and to the neighbors that live down the street from me, and that is what modern technological society is designed to achieve. This isn’t a conspiracy theory, because all it takes to see the proof is to look out your window. It’s hard to be Catholic when we are made to belong to where we live and we cannot even break bread with our neighbors. Of course, it is difficult to be Catholic in any age; it’s not like getting to heaven is any harder than it ever has been. But as Dorothy Day says, “God meant things to be much easier than we have made them,” and as her friend and fellow Catholic Worker Peter Maurin stressed, part of the aim of the Catholic Church is to cultivate society in such a way that it is easier for people to be good. Is it too much to wonder, as some already have, whether contemporary culture is diametrically opposed to Christianity? It was Berry’s writing that first led me on this path of inquiry, and it has made me a better (if still woefully bad) Catholic.

* * *

Berry is one of those totalizing writers whose worldview is easy to apply to everything, similar to thinkers like René Girard. Many, myself included, have been inspired at one time or another to adopt a Berrian style, emulating his project in a performative way but not a substantive one, lamenting the absence of real community but not really making the heavy sacrifices necessary to cultivate it, grieving over the destruction of vast swaths of land while failing to care for the soil in my own backyard, et cetera. I hope Berry never had the misfortune of encountering the term “aura farming,” and I shudder to think there could be someone out there doing such a thing on his account. Berry would, I suspect, just shake his head and keep picking tobacco. We don’t get anything done by peddling sentiments.

* * *

Through Berry, I have come to understand that salvation is not vague: One is never saved in a vacuum, in some obscure part of the person that we never perceive. Rather, the work of salvation is done on the land, in a particular place, within a concrete community. The sacraments are always performed in person. Whether you get saved depends, in part, on what you did or did not do where you live. Redemption in Christ is not divorced from the earth. He allowed us to bury him in it.

* * *

Pater meus agricola est. “My Father is a farmer” (John 15:1).1 Do we not know that we must be about our Father’s business?

1 I’m grateful to Jason Craig, an ardent reader of Wendell Berry, for first drawing my attention to the Vulgate text of this verse.

items.title: Blessed Is He: The Life and Legacy of Archbishop Fulton J. Sheen
items.author: Dr. Richard DeClue
items.summary:
Dr. Richard DeClue

Ven. Fulton J. Sheen will be beatified on September 24, 2026. Here is an overview of this holy bishop’s life and accomplishments.
items.content:
📖 Catholic Teaching | Word on Fire

Dr. Richard DeClue

Ven. Fulton J. Sheen will be beatified on September 24, 2026, in St. Louis, Missouri. As a fan of Archbishop Fulton Sheen since my childhood, I was thrilled to hear this news! Looking forward to that event, I would like to give an overview of this holy bishop’s life and accomplishments. 

Fulton Sheen was born in El Paso, IL, in 1895. I only recently learned from the Archbishop Fulton J. Sheen Foundation that his given name at birth was actually Peter John Sheen. However, while still a child, he began to be called Fulton, which was his mother’s maiden name. He was raised in the Catholic faith and was always devoted to Our Blessed Mother.

Fulton was high school valedictorian, graduating from Spalding Institute (a Catholic high school in Peoria, IL) in 1913. Thereafter, he attended St. Viator College before becoming a seminarian for the Diocese of Peoria. He was ordained to the priesthood on September 20, 1919. The next year, he began further studies at the Catholic University of America (CUA), earning an ecclesiastical degree in canon law (J.C.B.). The following year, he moved to the Catholic University of Louvain (Belgium), where he earned a PhD in philosophy in 1923, winning the Cardinal Mercier Prize for International Philosophy. In 1924, he earned the degree of Doctor of Sacred Theology at the Pontifical University of St. Thomas Aquinas in Rome (a.k.a., the Angelicum).

According to the Encyclopedia Britannica, Sheen then spent another year of study in Belgium, followed by a year of priestly ministry in London. He returned to his home diocese and worked as a parish priest in 1926. That same year, however, he joined the faculty at CUA.

As the university’s Fulton Sheen biography states: “For the next 23 years, Catholic University was where Father Sheen honed his skills as a scholar, educator, orator and evangelist. He worked, first in the School of Theology and Religious Studies, then in the School of Philosophy.” He taught courses such as “Philosophy of Religion,” “God and Society,” and “God and Modern Philosophy.” During this time, he was given the title of monsignor by Pope Pius XI in 1934 at the age of thirty-nine.

While still undertaking his professorial duties, Sheen did not remain in the ivory tower of academia. Known for his skills as an orator, Sheen expanded his reach through a weekly radio program, The Catholic Hour, starting in 1930 and lasting for about twenty-two years with an estimated audience of four million listeners.

In 1951, Fulton Sheen was consecrated as an Auxiliary Bishop of the Archdiocese of New York. That same year, he started his weekly television program, Life is Worth Living, which is probably what he is most known for today. Within a couple of months, the number of stations carrying his program jumped from three to fifteen. “Over the course of the show, Sheen’s Life is Worth Living competed for airtime with popular television stars such as Frank Sinatra and Milton Berle. . . . and in 1953, just two years after its debut, he won an Emmy Award for ‘Most Outstanding Television Personality.’” Apparently, his show, which ran until 1957, had a weekly viewership of a staggering 30 million!

On October 21, 1956, Bishop Sheen appeared on a popular game show What’s My Line? as a mystery guest. The purpose was to raise money for 300 leper colonies run by the Society for the Propagation of the Faith, for which Sheen became the director in 1958.

From 1961 to 1969, “he hosted another popular television show, The Bishop Fulton Sheen Show.” In the middle of that time period, he participated in every session of the Second Vatican Council (1962–1965). According to the CUA website, “he worked closely with then Father Joseph Ratzinger, who was a theological expert on the commission for mission.” During Ratzinger’s tenure as pope, he spoke of how “‘Fulton Sheen . . . would fascinate us in the evenings with his talks.’” Benedict XVI declared Fulton Sheen “Venerable” in July 2012. 

Following the council, Sheen was appointed as Bishop of Rochester, NY, in 1966, serving until 1969 when he resigned at the age of seventy-four, a year before the standard retirement age. As Matthew McDonald reports, “Sheen’s three years in Rochester were difficult.” He had tried to donate “a lightly attended inner-city parish church and its land for a federal public housing project for poor people,” but it “drew so much opposition that parishioners threw pebbles at his car when he visited.”

A man of principle, he received backlash from the right and the left. On the one hand, Bishop Sheen met with resistance from the local faithful who did not agree with his manner of implementing the reforms of Vatican II. On the other, “he also drew fire when he defended Pope Paul VI’s anti-contraception encyclical Humanae Vitae,” McDonald notes. Additionally, he was against the United States of America’s involvement in the Vietnam War as well as strongly opposed to Communism.

After his resignation from Rochester, he was named titular Archbishop of Newport, Wales. “From 1976 until his death three years later,” according to Encyclopedia Britannica, “Sheen served Pope Paul VI as assistant to the Pontifical Throne. . . . he died shortly after open-heart surgery in 1979 at the age of 84.”

Fulton J. Sheen’s work and legacy extend far beyond his mass media presence. As CUA records: “He published 34 books during his 23-year teaching career . . . and another 32 after he left the University.” A list of these books, in chronological order of publication, can be found here. Furthermore, “he also was a syndicated columnist in the secular press.”

Sheen’s public notoriety, however, is not even the most admirable aspect of his sanctity. “Admirers of Sheen see markers of holiness throughout his life, including his charity (he gave away millions in royalties, salary and gifts); his concern for troubled souls (he would drop everything to help a single person in need); and his Holy Hour, a 60-minute time in prayer before the Blessed Sacrament that he performed every day,” writes McDonald.

Ven. Fulton J. Sheen’s charity and good work did not end with his death. As a standard requirement for beatification, a miraculous healing has been attributed to his intercession. As reported by Joseph Pronechen, the miracle occurred on September 16, 2010. A baby boy had been stillborn to parents Travis and Bonnie Engstrom from Peoria, IL. The family and friends of the baby’s parents had been imploring Archbishop Fulton Sheen’s intercession since the birth began. Two medical professionals present at the home-birth tried to provide emergency help, but nothing was working. The boy’s father conducted an emergency baptism, naming him James Fulton, after the late bishop. The infant was rushed to the hospital, “where medical professionals tried every possibility to revive and save him. But with no pulse or sign of life after 61 minutes, and doctors about to record his time of death, James [Fulton] came to life.”

While the doctors were obviously astounded at this miraculous return to life, they still gave a poor prognosis. They said that, because he must have suffered “massive organ damage . . . [he] would soon die,” writes Pronechon. When that did not happen either, they were certain he would at least be “severely handicapped.” Afterall, an MRI showed brain damage from the lack of oxygen. Yet, three months later, at a follow-up examination, his brain scans were normal. Now, eight days after his sixteenth birthday, James Fulton Engstrom and his parents will attend the beatification of the holy archbishop, whose own life has inspired multiple generations of Catholic faithful.
